1.desc: Linux, Windows, macOS endpoint and server monitoring — CPU, memory, disk, processes, security events, and compliance.
1.quick: Deploy Splunk_TA_nix or Splunk_TA_windows on forwarders to start collecting OS metrics immediately.

10.desc: Next-gen firewalls, IDS/IPS, endpoint protection, email security, web security, vulnerability management, SIEM & SOAR, and certificate/PKI — threat detection and SecOps. ESCU detections are distributed across subcategories 10.1–10.8.
10.quick: Forward firewall logs (syslog) and install the vendor TA (Palo Alto, Fortinet, etc.). Use `import_sse_detections.py` to import ESCU detections, then `redistribute_sse_ucs.py` to place them in the right subcategories.

11.desc: Microsoft 365, Exchange, Teams, and collaboration platforms — mail flow, audit logging, and DLP events.
11.quick: Configure Splunk Add-on for Microsoft 365 with Management Activity API for audit events.

12.desc: Source control, CI/CD pipelines, artifact management, and IaC — build failures, deployment frequency, and secret exposure.
12.quick: Forward CI/CD logs (Jenkins, GitHub Actions) via webhook or log file monitoring to Splunk.

13.desc: Splunk platform health, APM, synthetic monitoring, and log aggregation — indexer queues, search performance, and forwarder health.
13.quick: Use the Monitoring Console (MC) built into Splunk and supplement with _internal index searches.

14.desc: Building management, industrial control, Splunk Edge Hub, and IoT platforms — sensor data, anomaly detection, and OT security.
14.quick: Deploy Splunk Edge Hub with built-in sensors or configure MQTT/OPC-UA/Modbus protocol collection.

15.desc: Power/UPS, cooling/CRAC, and environmental monitoring — battery health, thermal management, and physical security.
15.quick: Integrate DCIM or BMS platforms via SNMP or API to collect environmental and power data.

16.desc: Ticketing systems and CMDB — incident trends, SLA compliance, MTTR, and change management correlation.
16.quick: Use Splunk Add-on for ServiceNow or REST API integration to pull ticket and CMDB data.

17.desc: NAC (802.1X), micro-segmentation, and SASE — network access control, posture assessment, and zero trust enforcement.
17.quick: Collect ISE/NAC RADIUS accounting logs and install Splunk_TA_cisco-ise for structured data.

18.desc: Cisco ACI, NSX-T, and software-defined networking — fabric health, policy compliance, and endpoint tracking.
18.quick: Install Splunk Add-on for Cisco ACI and connect to APIC for fault, event, and audit data.

19.desc: Cisco UCS, Nutanix, and hyper-converged infrastructure — blade health, service profiles, and hardware faults.
19.quick: Install vendor TA (UCS Manager, Nutanix Prism) and configure XML API or REST collection.

2.desc: VMware vSphere, Hyper-V, and KVM virtual infrastructure — host contention, VM sprawl, and capacity planning.
2.quick: Install Splunk Add-on for VMware and connect to vCenter to pull ESXi host and VM performance data.

20.desc: Cloud cost monitoring and capacity planning — spend trends, idle resources, rightsizing, and budget alerts.
20.quick: Ingest cloud billing data (AWS CUR, Azure Cost Management) and use Splunk for trend analysis.

21.desc: Industry-specific operational monitoring — energy, manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, oil & gas, retail, aviation, telecom, water utilities, and insurance.
21.quick: Combine standard infrastructure TAs with industry-specific data sources (SCADA historians, HL7 feeds, fleet telematics, POS systems) for vertical-specific observability.

22.desc: Cross-industry regulatory compliance monitoring — GDPR, NIS2, DORA, CCPA, MiFID II, ISO 27001, NIST CSF, and SOC 2. Deployable SPL for PII detection, breach notification timelines, data subject rights tracking, ICT risk management, and continuous control evidence.
22.quick: Map ES correlation searches and risk scores to specific regulatory articles for auditable, data-driven compliance evidence.

23.desc: Business-aligned analytics for non-technical stakeholders — customer experience, revenue & sales, marketing ROI, HR & people, supply chain, finance, customer support, executive KPIs, and ESG sustainability reporting.
23.quick: Use DB Connect to ingest CRM, ERP, and HRIS data alongside web logs and app telemetry for unified business intelligence in Splunk.

3.desc: Docker, Kubernetes, OpenShift container platforms — crash loops, OOM kills, resource limits, and orchestration health.
3.quick: Deploy Splunk Connect for Kubernetes (SCK) to ingest container logs and cluster events.

4.desc: AWS, Azure, GCP cloud infrastructure — API auditing, cost anomalies, resource drift, and security posture.
4.quick: Enable CloudTrail/Activity Log and use the respective Splunk TA to start collecting API audit events.

5.desc: Routers, switches, firewalls, load balancers, wireless, SD-WAN, and Meraki — interface health, routing, and traffic.
5.quick: Configure syslog from network devices to Splunk. Install Splunk Add-on for Cisco or vendor-specific TA.

6.desc: SAN, NAS, object storage, and backup systems — capacity trends, latency, IOPS, and backup job monitoring.
6.quick: Install vendor TAs (NetApp, Pure Storage, etc.) and configure REST API or syslog collection.

7.desc: SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and data platforms — slow queries, deadlocks, replication, and connection pools.
7.quick: Install Splunk DB Connect or vendor TA to collect database logs and performance metrics.

8.desc: Web servers, application servers, message queues, CDNs, and DNS — HTTP errors, response times, and SSL certificates.
8.quick: Forward web server access/error logs and install the appropriate TA for structured field extraction.

9.desc: Active Directory, Entra ID, LDAP, MFA, and PAM — authentication failures, privilege escalation, and identity governance.
9.quick: Enable Windows Security Event Log collection from DCs with Splunk_TA_windows for immediate AD visibility.

ucs.t: Splunk UF for macOS, custom scripted inputs

ucs.v: Unencrypted endpoints are a data breach risk if lost or stolen. Compliance requirement for most security frameworks (SOC2, ISO27001, PCI).

ucs.ge: Disabled Gatekeeper or System Integrity Protection weakens macOS security posture — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.v: Disabled Gatekeeper or System Integrity Protection weakens macOS security posture. May indicate developer override or tampering.

cmp.ea: Saved search 'UC-1.3.4' running on Custom scripted input (softwareupdate -l, sw_vers), archived to the restricted audit_evidence index (default 7-year retention). Auto-drafted — SME review required.

ucs.v: Unpatched macOS endpoints are vulnerable. Tracking update levels across the fleet supports vulnerability management.

ucs.v: Verify Gatekeeper and XProtect are enabled and definitions are current. Disabled or outdated security controls increase malware risk.

ucs.d: IPMI sensor data via scripted input, `sourcetype=ipmi:sensor` (custom)
ucs.ge: Temperature, voltage, and fan speed anomalies predict impending hardware failures before they cause unplanned downtime — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.v: Temperature, voltage, and fan speed anomalies predict impending hardware failures before they cause unplanned downtime.

ucs.ge: A degraded RAID has lost redundancy — another disk failure means data loss — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.v: A degraded RAID has lost redundancy — another disk failure means data loss. Requires immediate attention.

ucs.d: IPMI SEL (System Event Log) via scripted input, syslog from BMC
ucs.ge: Lost power supply redundancy means a single PSU failure away from an unplanned outage — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.t: Custom scripted input (`ipmitool`), SNMP, vendor management syslog (iLO/iDRAC)
ucs.v: Lost power supply redundancy means a single PSU failure away from an unplanned outage. Replacement needs to happen before the remaining PSU fails.

ucs.ge: SMART attributes can predict disk failure days or weeks in advance, enabling proactive replacement during maintenance windows — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.v: SMART attributes can predict disk failure days or weeks in advance, enabling proactive replacement during maintenance windows.

ucs.d: BMC/BIOS version data via scripted input
ucs.ge: Outdated firmware may have security vulnerabilities or known bugs — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.v: Outdated firmware may have security vulnerabilities or known bugs. Fleet-wide firmware tracking supports patch management.

ucs.ge: Correctable ECC errors that increase over time strongly predict impending DIMM failure — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.v: Correctable ECC errors that increase over time strongly predict impending DIMM failure. Proactive replacement avoids unrecoverable memory errors and system crashes.

ucs.d: `ipmitool lan print`, BMC health sensors, SNMP (if BMC supports it)
ucs.ge: BMC (IPMI/iDRAC/iLO) loss prevents remote power, console, and sensor access — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.v: BMC (IPMI/iDRAC/iLO) loss prevents remote power, console, and sensor access. Early detection ensures out-of-band management remains available for recovery.

cmp.co: Evidence that PCI DSS unknown is enforced — Splunk UC-1.4.8: PCIe Link Width and Speed Degradation.
cmp.ea: Saved search 'UC-1.4.8' running on lspci -vv, /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/current_link_width_speed, archived to the restricted audit_evidence index (default 7-year retention). Auto-drafted — SME review required.

ucs.ge: PCIe links that downgrade (x16→x8) indicate slot or cable issues — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.n: PCIe Link Width and Speed Degradation
ucs.t: Custom scripted input (`lspci -vv` or Windows PCI query)
ucs.v: PCIe links that downgrade (e.g. x16→x8) indicate slot or cable issues. Affects GPU, NVMe, and HBA performance and can precede full failure.

ucs.ge: IPMI sensor events (temperature, voltage, fan) indicate environmental or hardware problems before they cause crashes — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.t: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (scripted input), IPMI
ucs.v: IPMI sensor events (temperature, voltage, fan) indicate environmental or hardware problems before they cause crashes. Critical for datacenter and server health.

ucs.ge: RAID/HBA controller errors and degraded state often precede array failure — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.v: RAID/HBA controller errors and degraded state often precede array failure. Early visibility enables planned maintenance and avoids data loss.

ucs.d: `dmidecode -t bios`, vendor REST/CLI (iDRAC, iLO) for boot order
ucs.ge: Unauthorized or accidental boot order changes can prevent systems from booting from the correct disk or PXE — so you find out before users do when something is slowing down or breaking.
ucs.n: Boot Order and UEFI/BIOS Configuration Drift
ucs.v: Unauthorized or accidental boot order changes can prevent systems from booting from the correct disk or PXE. Tracking supports change audit and recovery.

ucs.ge: CPU ready time measures how long a VM waits for physical CPU — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: CPU ready time measures how long a VM waits for physical CPU. High values (>5%) mean the host is overcommitted and VMs are starved for compute.

ucs.ge: Memory ballooning means the hypervisor is reclaiming memory from VMs — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Memory ballooning means the hypervisor is reclaiming memory from VMs. Swapping at the hypervisor level is worse — causes severe VM performance degradation invisible to the guest OS.

ucs.ge: A full datastore prevents VM disk writes, causing crashes and corruption — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: A full datastore prevents VM disk writes, causing crashes and corruption. Datastores fill gradually from VM growth, snapshots, and log accumulation.

ucs.ge: Storage latency >20ms significantly impacts VM performance — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Storage latency >20ms significantly impacts VM performance. Detects SAN issues, datastore contention, or storage path problems before applications are affected.

ucs.ge: Old snapshots consume datastore space exponentially, degrade VM I/O performance, and complicate backups — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Old snapshots consume datastore space exponentially, degrade VM I/O performance, and complicate backups. Snapshots >72 hours old are generally a problem.

ucs.ge: We track VM migrations for troubleshooting and change management — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Tracks VM migrations for troubleshooting and change management. Excessive vMotion can indicate DRS instability or resource contention.

ucs.ge: HA failover means a host failed and VMs were restarted on surviving hosts — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: HA failover means a host failed and VMs were restarted on surviving hosts. Indicates hardware failure and potential capacity risk on remaining hosts.

ucs.ge: DRS should keep clusters balanced — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: DRS should keep clusters balanced. Frequent or failed DRS recommendations indicate resource constraints, affinity rule conflicts, or misconfiguration.

ucs.ge: Orphaned, powered-off, or idle VMs waste storage, IP addresses, backup capacity, and licenses — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Orphaned, powered-off, or idle VMs waste storage, IP addresses, backup capacity, and licenses. Regular cleanup frees significant resources.

ucs.ge: VSAN is the storage fabric for many VMware clusters — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: vSAN is the storage fabric for many VMware clusters. Degraded vSAN health can cause VM data loss and cluster-wide outages.

ucs.ge: -based hardware health detects physical component failures (fans, PSU, temperature) at the hypervisor level before they cause host failure — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: CIM-based hardware health detects physical component failures (fans, PSU, temperature) at the hypervisor level before they cause host failure.

ucs.ge: VMs consistently using <20% of allocated CPU/memory waste resources that other VMs could use — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: VMs consistently using <20% of allocated CPU/memory waste resources that other VMs could use. Right-sizing saves money and improves cluster capacity.

ucs.ge: Centralizing vCenter alarms in our monitoring platform reduces mean-time-to-repair during compound failures (datastore latency + host memory pressure) that appear as separate alarms in vSphere — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Centralizing vCenter alarms in Splunk reduces mean-time-to-repair during compound failures (e.g. datastore latency + host memory pressure) that appear as separate alarms in vSphere. Alarm storm correlation by shared datastore or maintenance window prevents alert fatigue and highlights the root cause rather than symptoms.

ucs.ge: Unpatched ESXi hosts have known vulnerabilities — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Unpatched ESXi hosts have known vulnerabilities. Fleet-wide version tracking ensures consistent patching and audit compliance.

ucs.ge: We track VM lifecycle for change management compliance and resource governance — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Tracks VM lifecycle for change management compliance and resource governance. Detects unauthorized VM creation or suspicious deletions.

ucs.ge: Dropped packets at the vNIC level indicate network saturation, driver issues, or misconfigured traffic shaping policies — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: VM Network I/O and Dropped Packets
ucs.v: Dropped packets at the vNIC level indicate network saturation, driver issues, or misconfigured traffic shaping policies. Unlike guest OS network stats, hypervisor-level counters capture drops the VM never sees — making this the only reliable way to detect silent packet loss that degrades application performance.

ucs.ge: We track read/write IOPS per VM to identify storage-hungry workloads before they impact other VMs on the same datastore — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: VM Disk IOPS Trending and Throttling
ucs.v: Tracks read/write IOPS per VM to identify storage-hungry workloads before they impact other VMs on the same datastore. When Storage I/O Control (SIOC) throttles a VM, it appears as increased latency inside the guest — this use case exposes the throttling at the hypervisor level.

ucs.ge: Outdated or missing VMware Tools causes loss of guest-host integration — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: VMware Tools Status and Version Compliance
ucs.v: Outdated or missing VMware Tools causes loss of guest-host integration — no graceful shutdown, no quiesced snapshots, no balloon driver, degraded network/disk performance, and inaccurate guest OS reporting. Tools must be current for vMotion to function optimally.

ucs.d: `sourcetype=vmware:events`, VDS health check results, vCenter network events
ucs.ge: VDS port errors indicate network segments misconfiguration, MTU mismatches, uplink failures, or teaming policy problems — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: Distributed vSwitch Port Health and Errors
ucs.v: VDS port errors indicate VLAN misconfiguration, MTU mismatches, uplink failures, or teaming policy problems. VDS health check results (available since vSphere 5.1) detect common misconfigurations that cause intermittent connectivity issues that are extremely hard to troubleshoot from the guest OS.

ucs.ge: Resource pools with hard limits can silently throttle VMs even when the cluster has spare capacity — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Resource pools with hard limits can silently throttle VMs even when the cluster has spare capacity. Pools without reservations provide no guarantees during contention. Monitoring utilization vs. configured limits/reservations reveals misconfigurations that cause unpredictable performance.

ucs.ge: Unexpected ESXi reboots indicate hardware failure (memory ECC errors, CPU machine checks), kernel panics (PSODs), or firmware bugs — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Unexpected ESXi reboots indicate hardware failure (memory ECC errors, CPU machine checks), kernel panics (PSODs), or firmware bugs. Each reboot triggers HA failover of all VMs on that host, causing widespread service disruption. Early detection enables root cause analysis before the issue recurs.

ucs.d: `sourcetype=vmware:events`, vCenter VAMI health API, vCenter syslog (`/var/log/vmware/vpxd/vpxd.log`)
ucs.ge: VCenter is the management plane for the entire VMware environment — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: vCenter is the management plane for the entire VMware environment. If VPXD, SSO, or the content library service fails, you lose visibility into your VMs and cannot perform management operations. Monitoring vCenter appliance health ensures the control plane is operational.

ucs.ge: Unexpected VM shutdowns or resets indicate guest OS crashes, resource exhaustion, or unauthorized actions — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Unexpected VM shutdowns or resets indicate guest OS crashes, resource exhaustion, or unauthorized actions. Unlike planned maintenance, unplanned power state changes disrupt services without warning. Correlating with the initiating user distinguishes admin actions from automated or malicious changes.

ucs.ge: Clock drift on ESXi hosts causes VM time drift, Kerberos authentication failures, log correlation issues, and vSAN timing problems — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Clock drift on ESXi hosts causes VM time drift, Kerberos authentication failures, log correlation issues, and vSAN timing problems. NTP misconfiguration is a common root cause of intermittent authentication failures that are difficult to diagnose.

ucs.ge: SIOC throttles VM disk I/O when datastore latency exceeds thresholds (default 30ms) — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: SIOC throttles VM disk I/O when datastore latency exceeds thresholds (default 30ms). When SIOC activates, VMs experience injected latency that appears as slow storage from the guest perspective. Detecting SIOC activation reveals contention invisible from the guest OS.

ucs.ge: Older VM hardware versions lack support for newer features — vNVMe, UEFI secure boot, vTPM, higher vCPU/memory limits, and improved device emulation — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Older VM hardware versions lack support for newer features — vNVMe, UEFI secure boot, vTPM, higher vCPU/memory limits, and improved device emulation. Running mixed hardware versions complicates fleet management and limits what features you can enable cluster-wide.

ucs.ge: After a failed snapshot deletion, VMs can have orphaned delta disks that keep growing and degrading I/O performance — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: After a failed snapshot deletion, VMs can have orphaned delta disks that keep growing and degrading I/O performance. The "consolidation needed" flag indicates the disk chain is broken and needs manual intervention before it causes datastore exhaustion.

ucs.ge: Thin-provisioned disks start small but grow to their provisioned maximum as the guest writes data — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Thin-provisioned disks start small but grow to their provisioned maximum as the guest writes data. If the total provisioned size of all thin disks on a datastore exceeds physical capacity (over-provisioning), the datastore can fill unexpectedly. Tracking actual growth rate predicts when this will happen.

ucs.ge: Anti-affinity rules ensure redundant VMs (HA pairs, database replicas) run on different hosts — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: VM Affinity and Anti-Affinity Rule Violations
ucs.v: Anti-affinity rules ensure redundant VMs (e.g., HA pairs, database replicas) run on different hosts. Rule violations mean a single host failure can take down both instances. Affinity rules keep related VMs together for performance. DRS may violate rules when resources are constrained.

ucs.ge: Storage DRS (SDRS) balances VM storage across datastores within a datastore cluster — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Storage DRS (SDRS) balances VM storage across datastores within a datastore cluster. Frequent SDRS migrations indicate capacity or performance imbalance. Unapplied recommendations (when SDRS is in manual mode) mean datastores are unbalanced and latency may be inconsistent.

ucs.ge: VMware Fault Tolerance provides zero-downtime protection by maintaining a live secondary copy of a VM — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: Fault Tolerance Status and Replication Lag
ucs.v: VMware Fault Tolerance provides zero-downtime protection by maintaining a live secondary copy of a VM. If FT replication falls behind or becomes disabled, the VM loses its zero-downtime protection. FT lag indicates network bandwidth or CPU contention on the secondary host.

ucs.ge: ESXi hosts use certificates for secure communication with vCenter and other hosts — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: ESXi hosts use certificates for secure communication with vCenter and other hosts. Expired certificates cause vCenter disconnection, vMotion failures, and HA communication breakdowns. The VMCA-signed certificates have a 5-year default lifetime, but custom certificates may expire sooner.

ucs.ge: Lockdown mode restricts direct ESXi access, forcing all management through vCenter — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Lockdown mode restricts direct ESXi access, forcing all management through vCenter. Hosts not in lockdown mode can be accessed directly via SSH or the DCUI, bypassing vCenter audit trails and RBAC. Required by security frameworks like CIS, DISA STIG, and PCI DSS.

ucs.d: Custom scripted input (datastore file browser vs VM inventory comparison)
ucs.ge: When VMs are deleted without cleaning up their disk files, or when snapshots leave behind delta VMDKs, orphaned files accumulate and waste datastore space — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: When VMs are deleted without cleaning up their disk files, or when snapshots leave behind delta VMDKs, orphaned files accumulate and waste datastore space. In large environments, orphaned files can consume terabytes of storage that cannot be identified through normal VM inventory.

ucs.ge: VMware Tools reports guest OS filesystem utilization to vCenter, enabling disk space monitoring without-guest agent — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: VM Guest OS Disk Space via VMware Tools
ucs.v: VMware Tools reports guest OS filesystem utilization to vCenter, enabling disk space monitoring without an in-guest agent. Particularly valuable for appliances, embedded systems, and VMs where you cannot install a Splunk forwarder. Catches disk-full conditions before they crash applications.

ucs.ge: VM encryption protects data at rest on shared storage — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: VM encryption protects data at rest on shared storage. vTPM enables Credential Guard, BitLocker, and measured boot inside VMs. Compliance frameworks increasingly require encryption for workloads handling sensitive data. Tracking which VMs are encrypted vs. which should be ensures policy adherence.

ucs.ge: Stale VM templates with outdated OS patches, expired certificates, or old application versions get deployed into production and immediately become vulnerable — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Stale VM templates with outdated OS patches, expired certificates, or old application versions get deployed into production and immediately become vulnerable. Tracking template age and last update ensures new VMs start from a secure, current baseline.

ucs.ge: If ESXi syslog forwarding breaks, you lose visibility into host-level events — PSOD messages, hardware errors, authentication attempts, and kernel warnings — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: If ESXi syslog forwarding breaks, you lose visibility into host-level events — PSOD messages, hardware errors, authentication attempts, and kernel warnings. Since syslog is often the only real-time data source from ESXi (vs. the polling-based TA), silent forwarding failures create dangerous blind spots.

ucs.ge: ESXi has a built-in firewall that controls which services are accessible — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: ESXi has a built-in firewall that controls which services are accessible. Overly permissive rules (e.g., SSH from any IP, open NFC ports) expand the attack surface. CIS benchmarks and DISA STIGs require specific firewall configurations on ESXi hosts.

ucs.ge: VMs that span NUMA nodes experience cross-node memory access latency — 2-3x slower than local access — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: VMs that span NUMA nodes experience cross-node memory access latency — 2-3x slower than local access. Large VMs (8+ vCPUs or 32+ GB RAM) are most affected. Proper NUMA alignment can improve performance by 10-30% for memory-intensive workloads like databases and in-memory caches.

ucs.ge: When an ESXi host experiences a PSOD (Purple Screen of Death), the coredump contains critical diagnostic information — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: When an ESXi host experiences a PSOD (Purple Screen of Death), the coredump contains critical diagnostic information. Without a properly configured dump target (network or local), the coredump is lost on reboot and root cause analysis becomes impossible. Particularly important for diskless/boot-from-SAN hosts.

ucs.ge: Measures time VMs wait for physical CPU — distinct from host utilization — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Measures time VMs wait for physical CPU — distinct from host utilization. High CPU ready time indicates over-committed CPU; VMs are queued waiting for scheduler time even when host CPU % appears acceptable. Critical for identifying latent contention invisible from guest metrics.

ucs.d: `sourcetype=vmware:perf:datastore` (datastore.totalReadLatency.average, datastore.totalWriteLatency.average — per VM when object is VM)
ucs.ge: Correlate VM disk latency to specific datastores to identify storage bottlenecks — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: VM Disk I/O Latency per Datastore
ucs.v: Correlate VM disk latency to specific datastores to identify storage bottlenecks. When multiple VMs on the same datastore show high latency, the datastore or underlying storage is the culprit rather than individual VM workload.

ucs.d: Certificate expiry from ESXi hosts (scripted input querying host API or certificate store)
ucs.ge: ESXi hosts use secure connections certificates for vCenter communication, vMotion, and HA — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.t: Custom scripted input (openssl, ESXi API, or PowerCLI)
ucs.v: ESXi hosts use SSL certificates for vCenter communication, vMotion, and HA. Expired certificates break vCenter connectivity, prevent migrations, and cause HA communication failures. Proactive monitoring prevents unexpected outages when certs expire.

ucs.ge: Snapshots older than N days degrade VM I/O performance and complicate backups — distinct from snapshot count or space — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Snapshots older than N days degrade VM I/O performance and complicate backups — distinct from snapshot count or space. Old snapshots cause delta disk growth, extended backup windows, and increased risk of consolidation failures. Age-based alerting ensures timely cleanup.

ucs.ge: Track alarms that remain unacknowledged for extended periods — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: Track alarms that remain unacknowledged for extended periods. Unacknowledged alarms indicate ignored issues — either operational gaps or alarm fatigue. Ensures critical alerts receive follow-up and supports SLA tracking for incident response.

ucs.ge: -VM network quality metrics including packet loss and retransmission — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: VM Network Packet Loss and Retransmit
ucs.v: Per-VM network quality metrics including packet loss and retransmission. Dropped packets at the vNIC indicate congestion, driver issues, or misconfigured traffic shaping. Hypervisor-level counters capture drops invisible to the guest — essential for diagnosing application network issues.

ucs.ge: DRS migrations per hour, cluster imbalance score, and recommendations vs — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.v: DRS migrations per hour, cluster imbalance score, and recommendations vs. applied. High migration frequency may indicate oscillation; low application of recommendations suggests manual mode or constraint conflicts. Tracks whether DRS is effectively balancing the cluster.

ucs.d: `sourcetype=Perfmon:HyperV` (Hyper-V Virtual Machine Health Summary, Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor)
ucs.ge: -VM CPU, memory, and disk metrics identify resource contention and performance bottlenecks within the Hyper-V environment — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.

Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Per-VM CPU, memory, and disk metrics identify resource contention and performance bottlenecks within the Hyper-V environment.

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Replication lag means your DR site is behind. If replication breaks, you lose your recovery point objective (RPO).

ucs.ge: CSV issues can cause VM storage access failures across the entire cluster — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: CSV issues can cause VM storage access failures across the entire cluster. Redirected I/O mode significantly degrades performance.

ucs.ge: Audit trail for VM mobility — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Audit trail for VM mobility. Excessive live migrations may indicate cluster imbalance or storage issues.

ucs.ge: Outdated integration services cause performance issues and prevent features like time sync, heartbeat, and data exchange from working correctly — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Outdated integration services cause performance issues and prevent features like time sync, heartbeat, and data exchange from working correctly.

ucs.ge: Host-level CPU and memory utilization across all VMs determines capacity headroom — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Host-level CPU and memory utilization across all VMs determines capacity headroom. Unlike per-VM monitoring, host-level metrics reveal when the hypervisor itself is under pressure — affecting all VMs simultaneously. Tracks the root partition overhead which is invisible from within VMs.

ucs.ge: Dynamic Memory allows Hyper-V to adjust VM memory allocations based on demand — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Dynamic Memory allows Hyper-V to adjust VM memory allocations based on demand. When memory pressure is high, the host reduces VM allocations below their startup RAM — causing in-guest paging. Monitoring reveals whether Dynamic Memory is helping or hurting, and which VMs are being starved.

ucs.ge: Hyper-V checkpoints (snapshots) accumulate AVHDX differencing disks that grow over time and degrade I/O performance — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Hyper-V checkpoints (snapshots) accumulate AVHDX differencing disks that grow over time and degrade I/O performance. Old checkpoints complicate backup and recovery, consume unexpected storage, and cause merge storms when finally deleted. Production checkpoints are safer but still grow.

ucs.d: `sourcetype=Perfmon:HyperV` (Hyper-V Virtual Switch, Hyper-V Virtual Network Adapter)
ucs.ge: Virtual switch dropped packets indicate congestion, misconfigured network segments tagging, or bandwidth management policy throttling — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: Virtual Switch Dropped Packets and Network Errors

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Virtual switch dropped packets indicate congestion, misconfigured VLAN tagging, or bandwidth management policy throttling. Hyper-V Extensible Switch drops are invisible from within the VM, making hypervisor-level monitoring the only way to detect them.

ucs.ge: Hyper-V failover clusters require quorum to operate — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.
ucs.n: Failover Cluster Node Health and Quorum

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Hyper-V failover clusters require quorum to operate. A node leaving the cluster reduces fault tolerance and can trigger mass VM failover. Quorum loss means the entire cluster stops, downing all VMs. Monitoring node health and quorum status prevents catastrophic cluster outages.

ucs.ge: Storage Spaces Direct pools local storage across cluster nodes into a shared storage fabric — so you catch performance or capacity problems before they hurt real work.

predecessor.name: Splunk App for Unix and Linux
Splunk App for Windows Infrastructure

ucs.v: Traditional network monitoring in Kubernetes relies on service mesh sidecars or packet capture — both adding overhead and complexity. Cilium Hubble provides kernel-level L3/L4/L7 network visibility via eBPF without sidecar injection, capturing every network flow between pods, services, and external endpoints with near-zero performance impact. Ingesting Hubble flow logs into Splunk reveals unexpected service communication (security), DNS failures (availability), and packet drops (performance) that are invisible to application-level monitoring.

Tetragon provides kernel-level visibility into process execution, file access, network connections, and privilege escalation via eBPF tracing policies, with minimal overhead. Ingesting Tetragon events into Splunk enables correlation with application traces and infrastructure metrics — connecting "a process opened /etc/shadow" with "which user request triggered this" via trace context.

This provides instant observability for legacy services, third-party applications, and polyglot environments where manual instrumentation is impractical or too slow to roll out.

ucs.ge: Junos raises chassis alarms for power supply loss, fan failure, FPC or PIC offline, and temperature exceedances — conditions that often need on-site hardware work before service is fully restored — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.v: Junos raises chassis alarms for power supply loss, fan failure, FPC or PIC offline, and temperature exceedances—conditions that often need on-site hardware work before service is fully restored. Ignoring these events lets a single failed component escalate into switch-wide thermal shutdown or loss of redundancy. A clear Splunk view of major and minor chassis alarms speeds dispatch to facilities and vendor support and shortens mean time to repair for edge and campus fabrics.

ucs.ge: Junos treats configuration as a sequence of commits, so every change is tied to a user, time, and optional comment — ideal for audit and rollback to any of the last stored revisions — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: All Juniper Junos devices
ucs.n: Junos Commit History and Configuration Rollback Audit (Juniper)
ucs.v: Junos treats configuration as a sequence of commits, so every change is tied to a user, time, and optional comment—ideal for audit and rollback to any of the last stored revisions. Without central logging, you lose the evidence needed to prove who changed routing, security zones, or interfaces during an incident. Correlating commits with change tickets catches unapproved changes and commits outside maintenance windows before they propagate through routing or firewall policy.

ucs.ge: Platforms with dual routing engines rely on GRES and related state transfer; an unplanned mastership change usually means primary RE failure, kernel panic, or loss of control-plane stability — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Juniper MX240/MX480/MX960/MX2010/MX10008, EX9200, SRX5400/SRX5600/SRX5800
ucs.v: Platforms with dual routing engines rely on GRES and related state transfer; an unplanned mastership change usually means primary RE failure, kernel panic, or loss of control-plane stability. Repeated failovers on the same chassis point to degrading hardware or software defects before a hard outage. Tracking these events in Splunk gives operations a single place to justify RMA, software upgrade, or emergency maintenance.

ucs.ge: Virtual Chassis merges multiple switches into one control plane; a member disconnect or role churn can blackhole network segments or split forwarding across members — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.v: Virtual Chassis merges multiple switches into one control plane; a member disconnect or role churn can blackhole VLANs or split forwarding across members. VCCP and member state messages are the earliest signal of stack cable, power, or software issues. Centralized monitoring reduces time to detect partial stack failures that users report as intermittent “random” connectivity loss.

ucs.ge: MLAG pairs depend on matching configuration and a healthy peer link — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.v: MLAG pairs depend on matching configuration and a healthy peer link; inconsistency or peer loss can lead to blackholed VLANs or asymmetric forwarding while both switches appear “up.” Catching `config-sanity` failures and peer state changes early prevents subtle application outages that load balancers and servers cannot retry away from. Splunk correlation across both peers speeds root cause when only one side logs the fault.

ucs.ge: EOS features run as processes under ProcMgr; unexpected agent restarts often precede control-plane instability, STP or routing anomalies, or memory pressure — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.v: EOS features run as processes under ProcMgr; unexpected agent restarts often precede control-plane instability, STP or routing anomalies, or memory pressure. Tracking restart frequency by agent name ties platform symptoms to a specific subsystem instead of generic “switch is slow” tickets. Trending restarts after code upgrades also validates stability before promoting images fleet-wide.

ucs.d: CloudVision webhook JSON (HEC) or forwarded syslog from CVP
ucs.ge: CloudVision aggregates streaming telemetry and policy state across the fabric — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Arista CloudVision (on-prem or as-a-Service), all managed EOS switches
ucs.t: CloudVision webhook or syslog to Splunk HEC
ucs.v: CloudVision aggregates streaming telemetry and policy state across the fabric; forwarding those alerts to Splunk gives the NOC the same fabric-wide lens as the network team without logging into CVP for every spike. You can align telemetry-driven anomalies with application incidents and compliance audits. Historical alert volume also shows whether automation or drift is increasing operational noise.

ucs.d: Aruba CX syslog (`sourcetype=syslog` or site-specific parser such as `hpe:aruba` if configured)
ucs.ge: VSF stacks present one logical switch; member loss or conductor changes can isolate access network segments or reduce east-west capacity without a full box failure — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: HPE Aruba CX 6200, CX 6300, CX 6400, CX 8320, CX 8325, CX 8360
ucs.n: Aruba CX VSF Stack Health (HPE Aruba)
ucs.v: VSF stacks present one logical switch; member loss or conductor changes can isolate access VLANs or reduce east-west capacity without a full box failure. Early detection of member state changes and inter-switch link issues prevents prolonged segments of a floor or IDF running on a single surviving member. Splunk gives stack-level visibility where SNMP polling alone may lag during control-plane events.

ucs.d: Aruba CX syslog; SNMP traps (VSX / link state) if forwarded to Splunk
ucs.ge: VSX pairs use an inter-switch link and keepalive — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: HPE Aruba CX 8320, CX 8325, CX 8360, CX 8400, CX 10000
ucs.n: Aruba CX VSX Redundancy Monitoring (HPE Aruba)
ucs.v: VSX pairs use an inter-switch link and keepalive; if both fail, split-brain can leave two active primaries forwarding independently, risking loops, duplicate MACs, and hard-to-diagnose application errors. Monitoring ISL, keepalive, and synchronization state is essential for data center and campus cores where VSX fronts servers or downstream stacks. Splunk lets you alert before both control and data paths degrade past recovery.

ucs.ge: Citrix ADC (NetScaler) virtual servers (vServers) are the front-end load-balancing endpoints that distribute traffic to back-end service groups — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.n: Citrix ADC Virtual Server Health and State (NetScaler)
ucs.t: Splunk Add-on for Citrix NetScaler (`Splunk_TA_citrix-netscaler`), Splunk Connect for Syslog
ucs.v: Citrix ADC (NetScaler) virtual servers (vServers) are the front-end load-balancing endpoints that distribute traffic to back-end service groups. A vServer transitions from UP to DOWN when all bound services fail health checks, causing a complete outage for the application it serves. Monitoring vServer state changes provides immediate alerting when applications lose load-balanced availability.

ucs.ge: Behind each Citrix ADC vServer, service group members represent individual back-end servers — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.n: Citrix ADC Service Group Member Health (NetScaler)
ucs.v: Behind each Citrix ADC vServer, service group members represent individual back-end servers. When health monitors detect a service group member as DOWN, the ADC stops sending traffic to that server. A single member going down may be routine (maintenance), but multiple simultaneous failures indicate a systemic issue — network partition, shared dependency failure, or deployment problem. Monitoring service group member health identifies back-end server failures faster than application-level monitoring.

ucs.ge: Secure connections certificates on Citrix ADC terminate HTTPS connections for all web applications behind the load balancer — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.n: Citrix ADC SSL Certificate Expiration Monitoring (NetScaler)
ucs.t: Custom scripted input polling Citrix ADC NITRO API
ucs.v: SSL certificates on Citrix ADC terminate HTTPS connections for all web applications behind the load balancer. An expired certificate causes browser warnings or complete connection failures for all users. The NITRO API exposes `daystoexpiration` for every bound SSL certificate, enabling automated alerting well before expiry. Certificate expiry outages are among the most preventable yet impactful failures in production environments.

ucs.ge: Citrix ADC deployments typically use HA pairs where a secondary appliance takes over if the primary fails — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.n: Citrix ADC High Availability Failover Monitoring (NetScaler)
ucs.v: Citrix ADC deployments typically use HA pairs where a secondary appliance takes over if the primary fails. Failover events (PRIMARY → SECONDARY swap) are disruptive — active connections may be dropped, and if configuration sync was incomplete, the new primary may have a stale configuration. Monitoring failover events, sync status, and node health ensures HA is functioning correctly and that failovers are investigated promptly.

ucs.ge: Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB) distributes traffic across multiple data centers based on proximity, health, and load — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.n: Citrix ADC GSLB Site and Service Health (NetScaler)
ucs.t: Splunk Add-on for Citrix NetScaler (`Splunk_TA_citrix-netscaler`), NITRO API scripted input
ucs.v: Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB) distributes traffic across multiple data centers based on proximity, health, and load. GSLB relies on the Metric Exchange Protocol (MEP) between sites to share health and load metrics. If MEP connectivity fails between sites, the GSLB method falls back to Round Robin — potentially sending users to degraded or distant sites. Monitoring GSLB site health and MEP status ensures intelligent multi-site traffic distribution.

ucs.v: Citrix ADC appliances (physical or VPX) have finite CPU, memory, and throughput capacity. Unlike general-purpose servers, ADC resource exhaustion directly impacts all applications it fronts — causing connection drops, increased latency, and SSL handshake failures. Monitoring ADC system resources enables capacity planning and prevents appliance-level bottlenecks that affect the entire application delivery infrastructure.

ucs.ge: Responder and rewrite policies on Citrix ADC implement URL redirects, HTTP header manipulation, security rules, and custom error responses — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.

ucs.t: Custom scripted input polling Citrix ADC NITRO API
ucs.v: Responder and rewrite policies on Citrix ADC implement URL redirects, HTTP header manipulation, security rules, and custom error responses. Policy evaluation errors or undef (undefined) hits indicate misconfiguration — the policy expression failed to evaluate, causing the request to fall through to default behavior. This can result in bypassed security headers, missing redirects, or unexpected error pages being served to users.

ucs.ge: Citrix ADC offloads secure connections/secure connections processing from back-end servers, handling certificate exchange, cipher negotiation, and encryption/decryption — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.t: Custom scripted input polling Citrix ADC NITRO API
ucs.v: Citrix ADC offloads SSL/TLS processing from back-end servers, handling certificate exchange, cipher negotiation, and encryption/decryption. SSL transactions per second (TPS) is a capacity-bound metric — hardware ADC models have fixed SSL TPS limits, and VPX instances are licensed by throughput tier. Approaching the SSL TPS ceiling causes SSL handshake delays and new connection failures. Monitoring SSL performance ensures cryptographic operations do not become a bottleneck.

ucs.ge: Network signals polls interface counters every 5 minutes at best — microbursts and sub-minute congestion are invisible — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Cisco Nexus 9300/9500, Catalyst 9300/9500; Arista 7050X3/7060X/7260X3/7280R3/7500R3; Juniper QFX5120/QFX5220, MX204/MX304/MX480; Nokia SR Linux
ucs.n: Interface Utilization via gNMI Streaming Counters
ucs.v: SNMP polls interface counters every 5 minutes at best — microbursts and sub-minute congestion are invisible. gNMI SAMPLE subscriptions stream `/interfaces/interface/state/counters` at 10-30 second intervals, giving you near-real-time ingress/egress byte and packet rates. This catches congestion events that SNMP misses and enables capacity planning based on true peak utilization rather than averaged-out polling data.

ucs.d: gNMI path: `/interfaces/interface/state/counters` (in-errors, out-errors, in-discards, out-discards, in-fcs-errors), Telegraf metric: `openconfig_interfaces`
ucs.ge: CRC errors, input errors, and output discards often precede link failure or indicate a bad transceiver, duplex mismatch, or MTU issue — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Cisco Nexus 9300/9500, Catalyst 9300/9500; Arista 7050X3/7060X/7260X3/7280R3; Juniper QFX5120/QFX5220, MX204/MX304; Nokia SR Linux
ucs.v: CRC errors, input errors, and output discards often precede link failure or indicate a bad transceiver, duplex mismatch, or MTU issue. Streaming these counters at 30-second intervals via gNMI catches error bursts that 5-minute SNMP polls average away. A sudden spike in `in_fcs_errors` on a 100G spine link demands immediate investigation — it could be a failing optic about to take down a leaf.

ucs.ge: Syslog-based monitoring depends on log forwarding latency and parsing reliability — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Cisco Nexus 9300/9500 (NX-OS 9.3+), IOS XR (ASR/NCS); Arista 7050X3/7060X/7260X3/7280R3; Juniper MX204/MX304/MX480, QFX5120/QFX5220; Nokia SR Linux
ucs.n: BGP Peer State Change Detection via ON_CHANGE
ucs.v: Syslog-based BGP monitoring depends on log forwarding latency and parsing reliability. gNMI ON_CHANGE subscriptions to BGP neighbor state deliver sub-second notification when a peer leaves Established — faster than syslog and with structured data. For VXLAN EVPN fabrics where BGP is both underlay and overlay, a single peer drop can black-hole tenant traffic within seconds.

ucs.d: gNMI path: `/system/cpus/cpu/state` (OpenConfig), Cisco native: `Cisco-IOS-XR-wdsysmon-fd-oper:system-monitoring/cpu-utilization`; Telegraf metric: `openconfig_system`
ucs.ge: Network device control planes running hot indicate routing churn, excessive logging, or a control-plane DoS — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Cisco Nexus 9300/9500, IOS XR (ASR/NCS), IOS XE (Catalyst 9000); Arista 7050X3/7060X/7260X3/7280R3; Juniper MX/QFX/EX; Nokia SR Linux
ucs.n: System CPU and Memory Utilization Streaming
ucs.v: Network device control planes running hot indicate routing churn, excessive logging, or a control-plane DoS. gNMI streaming at 30-second intervals catches transient CPU spikes that 5-minute SNMP polls miss entirely. A Nexus spine hitting 90% CPU during a BGP convergence event could start dropping BFD keepalives, cascading into a fabric-wide outage.

ucs.d: gNMI path: `/components/component/transceiver/state` (output-power, input-power, laser-bias-current, temperature); Telegraf metric: `openconfig_platform`
ucs.ge: Optical transceivers fail gradually — Tx power drops, Rx power drifts, temperature climbs — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Cisco Nexus 9300/9500, Catalyst 9300/9500; Arista 7050X3/7060X/7260X3/7280R3; Juniper QFX5120/QFX5220, MX204/MX304; Nokia SR Linux
ucs.v: Optical transceivers fail gradually — Tx power drops, Rx power drifts, temperature climbs. By the time an interface goes down, the damage (packet loss, CRC errors, application impact) is already done. gNMI streaming of `/components/component` optic data at 60-second intervals enables predictive failure alerting: catch a dimming laser or overheating module hours before it causes an outage.

ucs.ge: Network signals-polled QoS counters miss microbursts entirely — a 100ms queue overflow causes packet loss that a 5-minute poll never sees — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Cisco Nexus 9300/9500 (NX-OS 9.3+); Arista 7050X3/7060X/7260X3/7280R3; Juniper QFX5120/QFX5220, MX204/MX304; Nokia SR Linux
ucs.n: QoS Queue Depth and Drop Streaming
ucs.v: SNMP-polled QoS counters miss microbursts entirely — a 100ms queue overflow causes packet loss that a 5-minute poll never sees. gNMI SAMPLE subscriptions to `/qos/interfaces/interface/output/queues/queue/state` at 10-second intervals capture queue depth and transmit/drop counters at a granularity that reveals microburst patterns, misclassified traffic, and under-provisioned queues.

ucs.v: In a properly cabled data center, the LLDP neighbor table should not change unless someone moves a cable, adds a device, or swaps a switch. gNMI ON_CHANGE subscriptions to `/lldp/interfaces/interface/neighbors` provide instant notification of topology drift — a new neighbor appearing on a spine port, a missing neighbor on a leaf uplink, or an unauthorized device connected to a reserved port.

ucs.ge: A sudden jump in received prefixes could indicate a route leak, hijack, or misconfigured peer advertising a full table into a leaf switch — so outages, slowdowns, and risky changes get flagged in time to act.
ucs.hw: Cisco Nexus 9300/9500, IOS XR (ASR/NCS); Arista 7050X3/7060X/7260X3/7280R3; Juniper MX204/MX304/MX480; Nokia SR Linux
ucs.n: BGP Prefix Count and Route Churn Monitoring
ucs.v: A sudden jump in received BGP prefixes could indicate a route leak, hijack, or misconfigured peer advertising a full table into a leaf switch. Conversely, a prefix count drop means routes are being withdrawn — potentially black-holing traffic. Streaming prefix counts via gNMI at 30-second intervals detects these events far faster than waiting for syslog or SNMP traps.

ucs.v: Environmental monitoring via SNMP Entity-MIB polling is slow and often unreliable. gNMI streaming of `/components/component/state` provides real-time temperature, fan speed, and power supply status. ucs.ge: The OTel Collector is a single point of failure for observability data — so you always trust the numbers you are looking at.
ucs.n: OpenTelemetry Collector Pipeline Throughput and Backpressure
ucs.t: Splunk Distribution of OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus remote write, custom HEC
ucs.v: The OTel Collector is a single point of failure for observability data. When exporters can't keep up with receiver intake, the batch processor queue fills and backpressure propagates upstream — first dropping low-priority data, then refusing new data entirely. By the time you notice missing traces in your backend, thousands of spans are already lost. Monitoring pipeline throughput and queue saturation in real-time catches backpressure within minutes, before it becomes data loss.

ucs.ge: OTel Collectors are Go processes that can OOM-kill under sustained load or memory leaks, especially with processors like or that hold data in memory — so you always trust the numbers you are looking at.
ucs.n: OpenTelemetry Collector Memory and CPU Utilization
ucs.v: OTel Collectors are Go processes that can OOM-kill under sustained load or memory leaks, especially with processors like `groupbytrace` or `tail_sampling` that hold data in memory. A killed collector creates a gap in observability data exactly when you need it most — during incidents. Tracking heap allocation growth patterns and CPU utilization catches runaway collectors before the OOM killer does.

ucs.v: In a fleet of dozens or hundreds of OTel Collector instances (DaemonSets, gateway deployments, agent sidecars), configuration inconsistency causes silent observability failures. One collector running a stale config may be missing a processor, dropping a signal type, or exporting to a decommissioned endpoint — while appearing healthy. Configuration drift detection ensures every collector runs the intended config after rollouts, preventing partial observability gaps.

ucs.v: Each OTel Collector receiver (OTLP, Jaeger, Prometheus, filelog, hostmetrics) independently accepts or refuses data by signal type (traces, metrics, logs). A receiver that starts refusing spans while accepting metrics indicates endpoint-specific authentication failures, protocol mismatches, or resource exhaustion on a single pipeline. Per-receiver, per-signal health monitoring pinpoints exactly which instrumentation endpoint is broken, reducing MTTR from "something is wrong with observability" to "the Jaeger receiver on collector-5 is refusing spans due to gRPC auth errors."

ucs.v: OTel Collector exporters retry failed sends with exponential backoff. Persistent retry failures indicate backend unavailability, authentication expiry, or network partitions. Monitoring retry counts and timeout rates per exporter and destination prevents the cascade where a slow backend fills queues, triggers backpressure, and ultimately causes data loss across all signals — not just the one with the failing backend.

ucs.n: Seq2Seq Log Anomaly Detection via Reconstruction Error (DSDL)
ucs.t: Splunk Deep Learning Toolkit (DSDL), custom Python container
ucs.v: Traditional log monitoring relies on known patterns — regex, keywords, error codes. But novel failures, zero-day exploits, and subtle misconfigurations produce log lines that have never been seen before. An LSTM or Transformer autoencoder trained on normal log sequences learns the "grammar" of healthy log output and flags lines with high reconstruction error — catching anomalies that no predefined rule could anticipate.

ucs.v: Infrastructure metrics (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network throughput) per host form a time × metric matrix that looks like an image. A Convolutional Neural Network trained on these "metric heatmaps" detects complex, multi-metric degradation patterns — such as the specific combination of rising CPU, flat memory, and oscillating disk I/O that precedes a particular failure mode — that univariate thresholds and even multivariate statistical models cannot capture.

ucs.ge: Simple error rate thresholds create two failure modes: too sensitive (alert on every transient error) or too lenient (miss sustained degradation) — so you always trust the numbers you are looking at.
ucs.n: SLO Definition and Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerting
ucs.t: Splunk Distribution of OpenTelemetry Collector, Splunk Observability Cloud
ucs.v: Simple error rate thresholds create two failure modes: too sensitive (alert on every transient error) or too lenient (miss sustained degradation). Google SRE's multi-window burn rate alerting solves this by measuring how fast you're consuming your error budget across multiple time windows. A fast burn (5min/1hr window) catches severe outages immediately; a slow burn (30min/6hr window) catches gradual degradation that compounds. This structured approach replaces ad-hoc threshold alerting with mathematically rigorous SLO-based alerting.

ucs.d: OTel Collector metrics, TSDB cardinality endpoints, `sourcetype=otel:metrics`
ucs.ge: Metric cardinality — the number of unique time series — is the hidden cost driver of observability platforms — so you always trust the numbers you are looking at.
ucs.t: Splunk Distribution of OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus, Splunk Observability Cloud
ucs.v: Metric cardinality — the number of unique time series — is the hidden cost driver of observability platforms. Adding a high-cardinality label like `user_id` or `request_id` to a metric can create millions of unique time series, overwhelming TSDB backends and causing query timeouts, memory exhaustion, and unexpected cost spikes. Detecting cardinality explosions before they impact platform stability prevents outages in the observability infrastructure itself.

ucs.ge: A service that stops emitting metrics or traces could mean two very different things: the service is down (infrastructure problem requiring immediate response) or the instrumentation broke (observability gap requiring engineering fix) — so you always trust the numbers you are looking at.
ucs.v: A service that stops emitting metrics or traces could mean two very different things: the service is down (infrastructure problem requiring immediate response) or the instrumentation broke (observability gap requiring engineering fix). Monitoring signal freshness — how recently each service last emitted each signal type — distinguishes these cases. If infrastructure monitoring shows the service is running but traces stopped, the instrumentation broke. If both stop, the service is likely down. Without freshness monitoring, instrumentation failures go unnoticed until the next incident when debugging tools fail.
